summary: AgentFlow is a static analyzer (built on the YASA engine) that recovers an Agent Dependency Graph from Python programs written against five agent frameworks (OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain/LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Semantic Kernel), modeling agents, prompts, models, tools/MCP/skills, memory and policy nodes. It is applied to Agent BOM generation and taint-style prompt-to-tool risk detection on AgentZoo, 5,399 GitHub agent projects.

claims.claim: AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than AST-based tools (Agent-Wiz, Agentic Radar)
claims.evidence: Table III on ADG-Eval (60 projects, 20 per framework): median 17 nodes / 28 edges vs 4/0 (Agent-Wiz) and 2.5/2 (Agentic Radar). 'Richer' is measured as raw counts with no ground-truth labeling of correctness or recall for RQ1, so more nodes could include false positives.

claims.claim: AgentFlow produces more dependency-aware Agent BOMs than Trusera, Drako and Cisco BOM tools
claims.evidence: Table V on BOM-Eval (100 projects): 2,295 components and 1,008 bindings vs 0 bindings for Drako/Trusera, 22 for Cisco. Baselines were not designed to emit binding relations, so the comparison is partly by construction; AgentFlow FP/FN inspection by two authors is mentioned but no BOM precision figure is reported in the read sections.

claims.claim: Uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world programs
claims.evidence: Table VI: 238 projects (4.4%) with 4,357 findings. Abstract wording '238 risks' actually means 238 projects. Manual audit of 100 reports: 73% precision (25 of 27 FPs due to sink semantics); 9 misses in 100 non-reported privileged agents. No exploitability confirmation or disclosure reported.
Median 14.17 s, p95 163.54 s per project on a 128-core/1 TB RAM server.

patterns.note: Typed dependency graph over agent components as a static IR; not used as agent context.
Static taint analysis from untrusted prompts to privileged tools finds risky paths at 73% precision on a 100-report audit.
Agent BOM as an inventory/audit artifact for governance.
Models control-policy/guard nodes in the ADG; does not evaluate guardrail effectiveness.
MCP servers and skills captured as capability nodes.

methodology.sample: AgentZoo: 5,399 Python GitHub projects; ADG-Eval 60 projects; BOM-Eval 100 projects; P2T-Audit 100 reported + 100 non-reported agents
methodology.baselines: Agent-Wiz, Agentic Radar (RQ1); Trusera-AI-BOM, Drako-Agent-BOM, Cisco-AI-BOM (RQ2); baselines are the existing open-source tools but solve a narrower problem
methodology.models: n/a (static analysis; no LLM in the analyzer)
methodology.variance: Deterministic tool; no inter-rater agreement reported for the two-author audits
methodology.languages: Python only (plus TypeScript checker code); five Python agent frameworks

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint, no venue in comment or journal_ref
standards.artifacts: No code or dataset release link found in the text; GitHub URLs are only to frameworks and baselines

biases.detail: RQ1/RQ2 treat larger node/edge/binding counts as better without ground-truth correctness for those counts.
BOM baselines are inventory tools that do not attempt binding relations; zero bindings is by design, not a failure.
Authors' tool, authors' sampled datasets, and authors' two-person manual audit for precision.
Only Python agent programs; acknowledged in §VI.
No release of AgentFlow, AgentZoo, or audit labels is stated.

verdict_reason: off-topic: analyzes the security/BOM of Python applications built on agent frameworks (LangChain, CrewAI, etc.), explicitly excluding coding agents like Claude Code; it does not inform how a Java team builds or runs a coding-agent harness. Evaluation is reasonable for its own scope but 'richer' is count-based and no artifacts are released.
applicability: Little transfer. The team's harness is coding agents operating on Java ingestion/delivery repos, not Python agent programs; AgentFlow does not analyze Java and excludes agent products. The only portable idea is conceptual: inventory which MCP servers/skills/tools each host config can reach and treat untrusted ingested healthcare content flowing into a prompt that can trigger write/exec tools as a taint path worth a policy check. That is better served by a deterministic config audit in the harness than by this tool.
